title: Three-Way Partition: Sort Colors
oneLiner: Sort an array of 0s, 1s and 2s in one pass with three pointers: everything before low is 0, everything after high is 2.
keyTakeaway: Keep three regions with three pointers: [0, low) holds 0s, [low, mid) holds 1s, (high, end] holds 2s, and mid scans the unknown middle. A 0 swaps to low (both advance), a 1 just advances mid, a 2 swaps to high (only high moves, because the value swapped in is still unknown). One pass, O(1) space.
explanation:
nums contains only 0, 1 and 2 (think red, white and blue). Sort it in place in a single pass and return it. Counting the three values and rewriting the array works in two passes; the classic interview answer is Dijkstra's Dutch national flag partition, which does it in one.

Maintain three pointers and four regions. Everything before low is 0. Everything from low up to mid - 1 is 1. Everything after high is 2. Between mid and high is still unknown. Start with low = mid = 0 and high = n - 1, and look at nums[mid] until mid passes high.

If it is 0, swap it with nums[low] and move both low and mid forward: the value that came back from low was a 1 (or this same 0), so it is already classified. If it is 1, it is already in the right region; just move mid forward. If it is 2, swap it with nums[high] and move only high back. Do not advance mid here: the value that just arrived from high has not been looked at yet.

Each step either advances mid or shrinks high, so the loop runs at most n times: O(n) time, O(1) space. This three-way partition is also what makes quicksort fast on arrays with many equal keys: partition into less than, equal to and greater than the pivot, and never recurse into the equal block.

The visualization runs [2, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0]. The tracker marks mid; highlighted cells are finished regions.

starterCode.python:
def sort_colors(nums):
    # TODO: low = 0, mid = 0, high = len(nums) - 1. While mid <= high:
    #   nums[mid] == 0: swap with nums[low], low += 1, mid += 1
    #   nums[mid] == 1: mid += 1
    #   nums[mid] == 2: swap with nums[high], high -= 1 (do not move mid)
    return nums

visualizationSteps.message: Start with low = 0, mid = 0, high = 5. Everything is unknown.
Saw 2: swap it to high and shrink high to 4. mid stays: the value that came back, 0, is not checked yet.
Saw 0: swap it to low, then advance low to 1 and mid to 1.
Saw 0: swap it to low, then advance low to 2 and mid to 2.
Saw 2: swap it to high and shrink high to 3. mid stays: the value that came back, 1, is not checked yet.
Saw 1: it belongs in the middle already. Advance mid to 3.
Saw 1: it belongs in the middle already. Advance mid to 4.
mid passed high, so nothing is unknown: 0s, then 1s, then 2s, in one pass.

recognitionSignals: Only three distinct values (or three classes: less than, equal to, greater than a pivot), sorted in place.
"One pass" and "constant extra space" on a partition problem.
gotchas: Advancing mid after swapping with high skips an unexamined value; that is the classic bug.
The loop condition is mid <= high, not mid < high: the element at high is still unknown.
high can go to -1 on an all-zero or one-element array; make sure that ends the loop instead of indexing.
confusableWith: Quicksort Partition (Lomuto) splits into two regions with two pointers; this splits into three with three.
Counting sort solves the same input in two passes by counting first; the three-pointer version does it in one and is what interviewers usually want.

complexity.note: Every step either advances mid or moves high back, so at most n steps in one pass; only three pointers are stored.
